about: MBBS0042 is the Year 1 run of UCL's five integrated Clinical and Professional Practice (CPP) modules: Anatomy and Imaging, Clinical Skills and Practical Procedures, Doctor as Data Scientist, Pathological Sciences, and Use of Medicines. These strands run vertically through all six years of the MBBS alongside the systems-based modules, and the Year 1 programme page lists MBBS0042 among the Year 1 modules. UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 assessment guide says the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests assess across modules and disciplines, including CPP teaching. UCL does not publish a separate Year 1 topic list for each strand, so this pack teaches standard foundation material for each strand and you should check coverage against the Year 1 Moodle learning objectives.

notes.h: Anatomy and Imaging: anatomical language and reading images
notes.body:
UCL does not publish a separate Year 1 syllabus for this strand, so this note covers standard foundation material that matches the official strand description; use the Year 1 Moodle learning objectives and the MBBS Curriculum Map to check exactly what your year covers.

What the strand is for
- UCL describes Anatomy and Imaging as building a working knowledge of normal and abnormal human structure and function, including how to interpret modern medical imaging.

Anatomical language
- Anatomical position: standing upright, facing forwards, arms by the sides with palms facing forwards, feet together. All directional terms assume this position, whatever the patient's actual posture.
- Planes: sagittal (divides into left and right; the median or midsagittal plane is in the midline), coronal or frontal (front and back), transverse or axial (upper and lower).
- Terms of relation: anterior (ventral) and posterior (dorsal); superior (cranial) and inferior (caudal); medial (towards the midline) and lateral; proximal and distal (along a limb, relative to its attachment); superficial and deep; ipsilateral (same side) and contralateral.
- Surface landmarks link anatomy to examination. For example, the sternal angle lies at the level of the second costal cartilages and roughly the T4/T5 intervertebral disc, a useful starting point for counting ribs.

Plain radiography (X-ray)
- X-rays pass through the body to a detector. Denser tissue absorbs more and appears whiter.
- The basic densities, from darkest to brightest: air (black), fat (dark grey), soft tissue and fluid (mid grey), bone or calcium (white), metal (brightest white).
- A border is visible only where two different densities meet. Loss of a normal border (the "silhouette sign"), for example of the right heart border, suggests that air in the adjacent lung has been replaced by something of soft-tissue density, such as consolidation.
- A chest film is usually taken posteroanterior (PA). An anteroposterior (AP) film, often taken in bed, magnifies the heart, so heart size should be judged on a PA film (a cardiothoracic ratio above about 0.5 suggests enlargement).
- Use a system: check the patient details and image quality first, then airway, lungs and pleura, heart and mediastinum, diaphragm, bones and soft tissues, and lines or tubes.

Computed tomography (CT)
- Uses X-rays from many angles to build cross-sectional images. Attenuation is measured in Hounsfield units: water 0, air about −1000, fat negative (around −100), bone strongly positive.
- Axial images are viewed as if from the patient's feet, so the patient's right is on the viewer's left.
- Gives far more detail than plain films but a substantially higher radiation dose.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
- Uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves, not ionising radiation. Excellent soft-tissue contrast (brain, spinal cord, joints).
- On T1-weighted images fluid is dark and fat bright; on T2-weighted images fluid is bright.
- Screening is essential: some implanted devices and metallic foreign bodies (for example in the eye) can be dangerous in the scanner.

Ultrasound
- High-frequency sound reflected from tissue interfaces. No ionising radiation, portable and real-time, so it is used in pregnancy and to guide procedures.
- Fluid is anechoic (black). Gas and bone block the beam, and image quality depends heavily on the operator.

Radiation protection
- In Great Britain, medical exposures are governed by the Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017 (IR(ME)R): every exposure must be justified and doses kept as low as reasonably practicable. Pregnancy status matters for exposures of the abdomen and pelvis.

Exam tips: in image questions, name the modality and the plane first, then describe what is abnormal using correct terms of relation and density, before suggesting a cause.

notes.h: Clinical Skills and Practical Procedures: safe foundations
notes.body:
UCL does not publish a separate Year 1 syllabus for this strand, so this note covers standard foundation material that matches the official strand description; use the Year 1 Moodle learning objectives and the MBBS Curriculum Map to check exactly what your year covers.

What the strand is for
- UCL's aim is that you become competent and confident in the practical skills and procedures set out in the GMC's Outcomes for Graduates (2018). That list includes, among others, measuring temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation; hand hygiene; venepuncture; intravenous cannulation; recording an ECG; capillary blood glucose; and urine dipstick testing. You are expected to perform these safely by graduation, building from simple skills in Year 1.

Before any skill
- Introduce yourself, confirm the patient's identity, explain what you will do, and gain valid consent. Respect privacy and dignity, and offer a chaperone for intimate examinations.
- Follow infection prevention practice, check the equipment, and afterwards document clearly and report any abnormal findings.

Hand hygiene
- The WHO's "My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene": before touching a patient; before a clean or aseptic procedure; after body fluid exposure risk; after touching a patient; and after touching the patient's surroundings.
- Alcohol hand rub is suitable for most situations, but use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled and when caring for patients with Clostridioides difficile or norovirus, because alcohol does not reliably kill spores or inactivate norovirus.
- Gloves do not replace hand hygiene: hands can be contaminated through tiny defects or when the gloves are removed.

Vital signs (adult)
- Pulse: feel the radial pulse for rate and rhythm, counting for a full minute if it is irregular. Assess character and volume at the carotid or brachial pulse. A resting rate of about 60–100 beats per minute is typical.
- Respiratory rate: count for a full minute (or 30 seconds × 2) without announcing it, since patients change their breathing when watched. About 12–20 breaths per minute is typical.
- Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry, and temperature.
- In the NHS these observations are combined in the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2; Royal College of Physicians, 2017). It uses respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, level of consciousness or new confusion, and temperature, plus whether the patient is on supplemental oxygen, to trigger escalation.

Manual blood pressure measurement
- The patient sits rested for a few minutes, with the arm supported at heart level and tight clothing removed.
- Choose the right cuff: the bladder should encircle most of the arm (about 80%). A cuff that is too small overestimates the pressure.
- Estimate the systolic pressure by palpating the radial pulse as you inflate. Then inflate to about 20–30 mmHg above that point and deflate slowly (about 2–3 mmHg per second) while listening over the brachial artery.
- The first Korotkoff sound (phase I) marks the systolic pressure; the disappearance of the sounds (phase V) marks the diastolic. Record the reading and the arm used.
- An arm held below heart level, or a rushed deflation, also gives errors.

Sharps and needlestick injuries
- Whoever uses a sharp disposes of it immediately into a sharps bin at the point of use. Never re-sheathe a needle.
- After a needlestick: encourage bleeding, wash with soap and running water (do not scrub or suck), and report urgently to occupational health or the emergency department, as post-exposure prophylaxis may be needed.

Basic life support (Resuscitation Council UK, adult)
- Check for danger and for a response; open the airway; look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds; call for help (999 or the hospital emergency number) and get an AED.
- Start chest compressions at 100–120 per minute and 5–6 cm deep, with 30 compressions to 2 breaths, and minimise interruptions.

Exam tips: in skills questions, the safety steps (identity, consent, hand hygiene, sharps, documentation) earn marks as surely as the technique itself.

notes.h: Doctor as Data Scientist: using evidence well
notes.body:
UCL does not publish a separate Year 1 syllabus for this strand, so this note covers standard foundation material that matches the official strand description; use the Year 1 Moodle learning objectives and the MBBS Curriculum Map to check exactly what your year covers.

What the strand is for
- UCL describes it as learning to access, understand and evaluate research evidence for decision-making and practice, together with an introduction to digital health and data-driven technology.

Evidence-based medicine
- Sackett and colleagues (BMJ, 1996) described evidence-based medicine as the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of the current best evidence in decisions about individual patients, integrating that evidence with clinical expertise. Later versions of the definition (for example Sackett and colleagues' 2000 textbook) make the patient's values and preferences an explicit third element.
- Frame a question with PICO: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome. Search sources such as PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library, and use guidelines such as NICE's.

Study designs
- Randomised controlled trial (RCT): random allocation balances known and unknown confounders, so it is the strongest single design for judging treatment effects.
- Cohort study: follows exposed and unexposed groups forward to compare outcomes. Suited to prognosis and to harms that would be unethical to assign at random.
- Case–control study: compares past exposures in people with and without a disease. Efficient for rare diseases; reports odds ratios.
- Cross-sectional study: a snapshot, giving prevalence.
- Systematic review and meta-analysis: a structured synthesis of all relevant studies.
- The traditional "hierarchy of evidence" (with systematic reviews of RCTs at the top) is a useful rule of thumb but is debated. The best design depends on the question, and a large, well-conducted observational study can be more informative than a small, biased trial.

Bias and confounding
- Selection bias: the groups differ systematically. Information (measurement) bias: outcomes or exposures are recorded inaccurately. Confounding: a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome.
- Protections include randomisation with concealed allocation, blinding, intention-to-treat analysis and complete follow-up.

Measuring treatment effects
- With control event rate (CER) and experimental event rate (EER): absolute risk reduction ARR = CER − EER; relative risk RR = EER/CER; relative risk reduction RRR = ARR/CER; number needed to treat NNT = 1/ARR.
- Example: CER 10% and EER 6% give ARR = 4 percentage points, RR = 0.6, RRR = 40% and NNT = 25.
- A relative reduction sounds impressive even when the absolute benefit is small, so report absolute risks to patients.

Diagnostic tests
- Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN), the proportion of people with the disease who test positive. Specificity = TN/(TN + FP), the proportion without the disease who test negative.
- Positive predictive value PPV = TP/(TP + FP); negative predictive value NPV = TN/(TN + FN). Predictive values depend on prevalence.
- Example: sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%, prevalence 1% in 10 000 people. Then TP = 90, FN = 10, FP = 495 and TN = 9405, so PPV = 90/585 ≈ 15% while NPV ≈ 99.9%. Most positives in a low-prevalence population are false.

Statistical inference
- A p-value is the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
- A 95% confidence interval gives a range of values compatible with the data. If the interval for a difference excludes 0 (or for a ratio excludes 1), the result is statistically significant at the 5% level.
- Statistical significance is not the same as clinical importance: look at the size of the effect.

Digital health and data
- Electronic health records, apps, remote monitoring and AI tools create large data sets. Questions to ask: was the algorithm validated on patients like mine? Is it biased against groups under-represented in its training data? Can its output be explained?
- Patient data are protected by UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 and, in health and care, by the Caldicott Principles (eight principles since December 2020; the eighth is about informing patients how their confidential information is used).

Exam tips: show the 2 × 2 table when calculating test statistics, always state whether a risk difference is absolute or relative, and interpret numbers in words.

notes.h: Pathological Sciences: cell injury, inflammation, thrombosis and neoplasia
notes.body:
UCL does not publish a separate Year 1 syllabus for this strand, so this note covers standard foundation material that matches the official strand description; use the Year 1 Moodle learning objectives and the MBBS Curriculum Map to check exactly what your year covers.

What the strand is for
- UCL describes Pathological Sciences as the theory and application of pathological science to clinical diagnosis and treatment. The core processes below underpin every system you study.

Cellular adaptations
- Hypertrophy: larger cells (for example left ventricular muscle in long-standing hypertension).
- Hyperplasia: more cells (for example the endometrium in the menstrual cycle).
- Atrophy: smaller or fewer cells (for example muscle that is not used).
- Metaplasia: one mature cell type replaced by another that copes better with the stress. Examples: bronchial columnar epithelium becoming squamous in smokers; in Barrett's oesophagus, squamous epithelium becoming glandular (columnar) under acid reflux. Metaplasia can progress to dysplasia and cancer.

Cell injury and death
- Reversible injury: cell swelling and fatty change. If the insult continues, injury becomes irreversible.
- Necrosis: uncontrolled death of groups of cells, with inflammation. Patterns include:
  - Coagulative: the outline of the tissue is preserved; typical of ischaemia in solid organs such as the heart and kidney.
  - Liquefactive: tissue is digested into fluid; seen in brain infarcts and abscesses.
  - Caseous: cheese-like; typical of tuberculosis.
  - Fat necrosis: as in acute pancreatitis.
  - Fibrinoid: in damaged vessel walls.
- Apoptosis: programmed, energy-dependent death of single cells, driven by caspases. The cell shrinks, the chromatin condenses and apoptotic bodies form, which are removed without inflammation. It is important in development and in removing damaged cells.

Acute inflammation
- The classic signs are redness, heat, swelling and pain (rubor, calor, tumor, dolor), with loss of function added later.
- Vascular changes: vasodilatation increases blood flow; increased vascular permeability lets a protein-rich exudate into the tissues.
- Cellular events: neutrophils marginate, roll (via selectins), adhere firmly (via integrins), migrate through the vessel wall and move along chemical gradients (chemotaxis) to phagocytose microbes.
- Mediators include histamine, prostaglandins, bradykinin and cytokines.
- Outcomes: resolution, suppuration (abscess), organisation with fibrosis, or progression to chronic inflammation.

Chronic inflammation and repair
- Chronic inflammation is dominated by macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells, with tissue destruction and repair happening at the same time.
- Granulomas are collections of activated (epithelioid) macrophages, often with multinucleate giant cells. Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis; non-caseating granulomas occur, for example, in sarcoidosis.
- Healing is by regeneration (where cells can divide) or by repair with granulation tissue and fibrous scar. Wounds heal by primary intention (edges brought together) or secondary intention (an open wound fills from the base).

Thrombosis, embolism and infarction
- Virchow's triad: changes in blood flow (stasis or turbulence), damage to the vessel wall (endothelial injury), and changes in the blood itself (hypercoagulability).
- An embolus is material carried in the blood that lodges at a distant site. Most are thromboemboli: a deep vein thrombosis can embolise to the lungs as a pulmonary embolus.
- An infarct is an area of ischaemic necrosis. White (pale) infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial supply, such as the heart, kidney and spleen. Red (haemorrhagic) infarcts occur in tissues with a dual blood supply or loose structure, such as the lung.

Neoplasia basics
- A neoplasm is an abnormal, autonomous growth. Benign tumours do not invade or metastasise; malignant tumours invade and can spread.
- Naming: carcinoma (epithelial) and sarcoma (connective tissue) are malignant; "-oma" alone usually means benign, but lymphoma and melanoma are malignant.

Exam tips: be precise with terms (metaplasia is not dysplasia; necrosis is not apoptosis), and link each process to a clinical example, because SBA stems are usually built around a patient.

notes.h: Use of Medicines: pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and prescribing safety
notes.body:
UCL does not publish a separate Year 1 syllabus for this strand, so this note covers standard foundation material that matches the official strand description; use the Year 1 Moodle learning objectives and the MBBS Curriculum Map to check exactly what your year covers.
This note covers principles only; it deliberately contains no drug doses. Always use the BNF and local guidance for real prescribing.

What the strand is for
- UCL describes Use of Medicines as learning to select the right drug, dose and duration for the right patient, while balancing pharmacology against other considerations, including economics.

Pharmacodynamics: what the drug does to the body
- Most drugs act on receptors, enzymes, ion channels or transporters.
- An agonist has affinity (it binds) and efficacy (it activates). An antagonist has affinity but no efficacy. A partial agonist cannot produce the full maximal response, however high the concentration.
- Potency is the concentration needed for a given effect (EC50). Efficacy is the maximum effect (Emax).
- A competitive antagonist shifts the agonist's dose–response curve to the right without lowering the maximum: its effect can be overcome by more agonist. A non-competitive or irreversible antagonist lowers the maximum.
- Therapeutic index: the ratio of toxic to effective dose. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index (for example digoxin, lithium and warfarin) need careful monitoring.

Pharmacokinetics: what the body does to the drug (ADME)
- Absorption and bioavailability: bioavailability is the fraction of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged (by definition 100% intravenously). Oral drugs may undergo first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver. Glyceryl trinitrate is given sublingually partly to avoid this.
- Distribution: the volume of distribution, Vd = amount in the body ÷ plasma concentration, is an apparent volume. Drugs that are highly tissue-bound can have a Vd far larger than total body water. Plasma protein binding also affects distribution.
- Metabolism: mainly hepatic. Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; often cytochrome P450 enzymes) are followed by phase II conjugation (for example glucuronidation), which makes the drug more water-soluble. Enzyme inducers (for example rifampicin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) lower the levels of drugs metabolised by those enzymes; inhibitors (for example clarithromycin) raise them.
- Excretion: mainly renal, so reduced kidney function lets renally cleared drugs accumulate.
- Clearance (CL) is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. The half-life is t½ = 0.693 × Vd/CL.
- With regular dosing, steady state is reached after about 4–5 half-lives, whatever the dose. A loading dose can reach the target concentration sooner.
- Most drugs show first-order kinetics (a constant fraction eliminated per unit time). When elimination saturates the kinetics become zero-order (a constant amount per unit time), as with ethanol, and small dose increases can then cause large rises in concentration.

Adverse drug reactions
- The Rawlins–Thompson classification: type A (augmented) reactions are predictable, dose-related extensions of the drug's pharmacology and are common; type B (bizarre) reactions are unpredictable and not dose-related, such as anaphylaxis or idiosyncratic reactions. Extended schemes add C (chronic), D (delayed), E (end of use or withdrawal) and F (failure of therapy).
- In the UK, suspected adverse reactions are reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme. Newer medicines under additional monitoring carry a black triangle (▼), and all suspected reactions to them should be reported.

Prescribing safely
- Check the patient's identity, allergies (and what the reaction was), weight where relevant, renal and hepatic function, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and all their current medicines, including over-the-counter and herbal products.
- Older patients are more vulnerable because of polypharmacy, reduced renal function and the risk of falls.
- Write clearly: approved (generic) names, route, frequency, duration and indication. Avoid dangerous abbreviations (for example write "units" in full).
- Cost matters: NICE assesses cost-effectiveness, typically as cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY), so that NHS resources do the most good.

Exam tips: be ready to explain an interaction or toxicity in terms of mechanism (enzyme induction or inhibition, reduced renal clearance, additive effects) rather than by memorising lists.

cards.b: Standing upright, facing forwards, arms at the sides with palms facing forwards and feet together; all directional terms refer to this position.
Sagittal: left/right (median plane in the midline). Coronal (frontal): anterior/posterior. Transverse (axial): superior/inferior.

cards.f: Five basic densities on a plain radiograph (dark to bright)
cards.b: Air, fat, soft tissue/fluid, bone (calcium), metal.
Loss of a normal border on a radiograph where two structures of the same density touch, e.g. lost right heart border from right middle lobe consolidation.

cards.f: Why judge heart size on a PA chest film?
cards.b: An AP film magnifies the heart because it is further from the detector; on a PA film a cardiothoracic ratio above about 0.5 suggests cardiomegaly.

cards.f: Hounsfield units of water and air
cards.b: Water 0 HU; air about −1000 HU; fat is negative; bone strongly positive.

cards.f: Which imaging modalities avoid ionising radiation?
cards.b: MRI and ultrasound. Plain radiography, fluoroscopy and CT all use X-rays.
Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017: medical exposures in Great Britain must be justified and optimised (doses as low as reasonably practicable).
Before touching a patient; before a clean/aseptic procedure; after body fluid exposure risk; after touching a patient; after touching patient surroundings.

cards.f: When is alcohol hand rub not enough?
cards.b: When hands are visibly soiled, and with C. difficile or norovirus: use soap and water, because alcohol does not reliably kill spores or inactivate norovirus.

cards.f: Korotkoff sounds for systolic and diastolic pressure
cards.b: Phase I (first sound) = systolic; phase V (disappearance of sounds) = diastolic.

cards.f: Effect of a blood pressure cuff that is too small
cards.b: It overestimates blood pressure, because more pressure is needed to compress the artery under a narrow bladder.
Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, systolic BP, pulse rate, level of consciousness or new confusion, temperature, plus whether the patient is on supplemental oxygen.

cards.f: First aid for a needlestick injury
cards.b: Encourage bleeding, wash with soap and running water (no scrubbing or sucking), and report urgently to occupational health or the emergency department.
100–120 per minute, 5–6 cm deep, ratio 30:2, minimal interruptions.

cards.f: Why count respiratory rate without telling the patient?
cards.b: People alter their breathing when they know it is being watched, which makes the count inaccurate.
Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome: a framework for turning a clinical problem into an answerable question.
NNT = 1/ARR, where ARR = control event rate − experimental event rate. CER 10%, EER 6% gives NNT 25.
Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN); specificity = TN/(TN + FP). Both are properties of the test and do not depend on prevalence.

cards.f: Why does PPV fall when prevalence is low?
cards.b: False positives from the large disease-free group outnumber true positives from the small diseased group, even with good specificity.
The probability of data at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true; not the probability that the null is true.
Distortion of an association by a third factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome; randomisation is the best protection.

cards.f: Best design to study a rare disease's risk factors
cards.b: Case–control study, comparing past exposures in cases and controls; it reports an odds ratio.
Eight principles (eighth added December 2020) for handling confidential health and care information, such as using the minimum necessary and only on a need-to-know basis.
Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another, e.g. squamous to columnar (glandular) epithelium in Barrett's oesophagus.
Necrosis: uncontrolled death of groups of cells with inflammation. Apoptosis: programmed, energy-dependent death of single cells by caspases, with shrinkage and no inflammation.
Tissue outline preserved; typical of ischaemic infarction in solid organs such as the heart and kidney.
Tissue digested into fluid; typical of brain infarcts and abscesses.
Abnormal blood flow (stasis/turbulence), vessel wall (endothelial) injury, and hypercoagulability of the blood.
A collection of epithelioid macrophages, often with multinucleate giant cells; caseating in tuberculosis, non-caseating in sarcoidosis.

cards.f: Steps of neutrophil emigration in acute inflammation
cards.b: Margination, rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins), transmigration, then chemotaxis to the site of injury.
White: solid organs with end arteries (heart, kidney, spleen). Red (haemorrhagic): dual blood supply or loose tissue, e.g. lung.
Agonist: affinity and efficacy (binds and activates). Antagonist: affinity without efficacy (binds and blocks).
Potency: the concentration needed for a given effect (EC50). Efficacy: the maximum achievable effect (Emax).
The fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged; 100% for intravenous administration.
Metabolism of an oral drug in the gut wall and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation, lowering its bioavailability.

cards.f: Time to reach steady state with regular dosing
cards.b: About 4–5 half-lives, independent of the dose; a loading dose can reach the target concentration sooner.

cards.f: Type A versus type B adverse drug reactions
cards.b: Type A: augmented, predictable, dose-related, common. Type B: bizarre, unpredictable, not dose-related (e.g. anaphylaxis).

cards.f: Effect of an enzyme inducer on another drug
cards.b: Induction of the metabolising enzymes (e.g. by rifampicin) speeds that drug's metabolism, lowering its levels and possibly its effect.
A constant amount eliminated per unit time because elimination is saturated (e.g. ethanol); concentrations can rise steeply with small dose increases.

questions.q: On a plain chest radiograph, which of these appears darkest?
questions.why: Air absorbs the fewest X-rays, so it is the darkest (black) density. Fat absorbs a little more and appears dark grey, not black. The heart is soft tissue and fluid, which appear mid grey. Bone such as the ribs contains calcium, absorbs strongly and appears white; choosing it reverses the rule that denser tissue looks brighter.

questions.q: On a CT scan, which substance has an attenuation close to 0 Hounsfield units?
questions.why: The Hounsfield scale is defined so that water is 0 HU. Air is about −1000 HU, the bottom of the usual range. Fat is negative (around −100 HU), because it attenuates less than water; choosing it assumes fat and water look the same. Cortical bone is strongly positive, often well over +1000 HU.

questions.q: Describe the anatomical position and define the three main anatomical planes. Explain why the anatomical position matters when describing a patient lying supine on a ward.
markScheme: Anatomical position: upright, facing forwards, arms at sides, palms forwards, feet together
Sagittal (median) plane divides into left and right
Coronal (frontal) plane divides into front and back; transverse (axial) plane divides into upper and lower
Directional terms always refer to the anatomical position, so descriptions stay consistent whatever the patient's actual posture (e.g. 'superior' still means towards the head when lying down)
questions.modelAnswer: In the anatomical position the body is upright and facing forwards, with the arms by the sides, the palms facing forwards and the feet together. The sagittal plane runs vertically from front to back and divides the body into left and right parts (the median plane is the one in the midline). The coronal or frontal plane is vertical and divides it into front and back. The transverse or axial plane is horizontal and divides it into upper and lower parts. Because all directional terms are defined relative to the anatomical position, a structure that is 'superior' is towards the head even when the patient is lying supine, so descriptions remain unambiguous between clinicians and on imaging reports.

questions.q: Which statement about hand hygiene in clinical practice is correct?
options: Wearing gloves removes the need for hand hygiene
Hand hygiene is needed after touching a patient's surroundings, even if you did not touch the patient
Alcohol hand rub is the best choice after caring for a patient with C. difficile diarrhoea
Hand hygiene is only needed when your hands look dirty
questions.why: Touching the patient's surroundings is one of the WHO's five moments, because the bed area becomes contaminated with the patient's organisms. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene: they can have tiny holes and hands are contaminated as gloves come off. C. difficile spores are not reliably killed by alcohol, so soap and water is needed. Hands can carry pathogens without looking dirty, so hand hygiene is needed at every one of the five moments, not only when soiling is visible.

questions.q: A student measures a patient's blood pressure with a cuff that is too small for the patient's arm. What is the most likely effect on the reading?
options: It will be unaffected if the patient is relaxed
Only the diastolic reading will be affected
questions.why: A narrow bladder has to be inflated to a higher pressure to compress the brachial artery, so it overestimates blood pressure. 'Falsely low' reverses this; an oversized cuff tends to underestimate instead. Relaxation reduces anxiety-related rises but does not correct the error from the wrong cuff size. The error affects both systolic and diastolic readings, not just diastolic.

questions.q: Describe how to measure blood pressure manually with a sphygmomanometer and stethoscope in an adult, including how you would avoid common errors.
markScheme: Introduce, identify, explain and gain consent; hand hygiene
Patient seated and rested, arm supported at heart level, correct cuff size (bladder encircling about 80% of arm)
Estimate systolic by palpation, then inflate about 20–30 mmHg above it
Deflate slowly (about 2–3 mmHg per second) listening over the brachial artery: phase I = systolic, phase V (disappearance) = diastolic
Record reading and arm used; errors avoided: small cuff or arm below heart level overestimates, fast deflation underestimates systolic
questions.modelAnswer: After introducing myself, confirming the patient's identity, explaining the procedure, gaining consent and cleaning my hands, I would have the patient seated and rested for a few minutes with the upper arm bare and supported at heart level. I would choose a cuff whose bladder encircles about 80% of the arm and place it with the bladder over the brachial artery. I would palpate the radial pulse while inflating to estimate the systolic pressure, deflate, then inflate to about 20–30 mmHg above that estimate. Listening over the brachial artery with the stethoscope, I would deflate at about 2–3 mmHg per second. The first Korotkoff sound (phase I) gives the systolic pressure and the disappearance of the sounds (phase V) gives the diastolic. I would record the reading and the arm used, and act on or report abnormal values. Common errors: a cuff that is too small, or an arm below heart level, overestimates blood pressure; deflating too quickly can miss the true systolic pressure; and skipping the palpation step can lead to missing an auscultatory gap.

questions.q: In a trial, 10% of patients in the control group and 6% in the treatment group have a stroke. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke?
questions.why: ARR = 0.10 − 0.06 = 0.04, so NNT = 1/0.04 = 25. 2.5 is 1/RRR, using the relative risk reduction of 40% instead of the absolute reduction. 17 is 1/0.06, the reciprocal of the treatment group's event rate alone. 10 is 1/0.10, the reciprocal of the control group's event rate alone.

questions.q: A screening test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. It is used in a population where 1% of people have the disease. Approximately what proportion of people who test positive actually have the disease?
questions.why: In 10 000 people, 100 have the disease (90 true positives) and 9900 do not (495 false positives), so PPV = 90/585 ≈ 15%. 90% is the sensitivity, the chance that a person with the disease tests positive, which is not the same as the chance that a positive person has the disease. 95% is the specificity. 99.9% is the negative predictive value, the chance that a person who tests negative is disease-free.

questions.q: Define sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value, and explain why a test with high sensitivity and specificity can still have a low positive predictive value when used for screening.
markScheme: Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN): proportion with disease who test positive
Specificity = TN/(TN + FP): proportion without disease who test negative
PPV = TP/(TP + FP): proportion of positive results that are true positives
PPV depends on prevalence; in screening the prevalence is low, so the many people without disease generate many false positives
Worked example or numerical illustration (e.g. 90%/95% at 1% prevalence gives PPV ≈ 15%)
questions.modelAnswer: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive, TP/(TP + FN). Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative, TN/(TN + FP). The positive predictive value is the proportion of positive results that are true positives, TP/(TP + FP). Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test, but PPV also depends on how common the disease is. In screening the prevalence is usually low, so even a small false-positive rate applied to the large disease-free group produces more false positives than there are true positives. For example, with sensitivity 90%, specificity 95% and prevalence 1%, 10 000 people give 90 true positives but 495 false positives, a PPV of only about 15%. This is why positive screening results need confirmatory testing and why patients should be counselled about false positives.

questions.q: In Barrett's oesophagus, what change occurs in the lining of the lower oesophagus?
options: Stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar (glandular) epithelium
Squamous cells increase in number but stay squamous
Disordered growth with nuclear atypia of the existing squamous cells
Columnar epithelium is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium
questions.why: Barrett's oesophagus is metaplasia: under chronic acid reflux, the normal stratified squamous lining is replaced by columnar (glandular) epithelium. Columnar to squamous is the reverse change, typical of the bronchi in smokers. An increase in cell number without a change of type is hyperplasia. Disordered growth with atypia describes dysplasia, which can develop later in Barrett's but is not the defining change.

questions.q: A patient has an ischaemic stroke. Which pattern of necrosis is characteristic of the infarcted brain tissue?
questions.why: Brain tissue has little supporting stroma and plenty of lipid, so ischaemic brain undergoes liquefactive necrosis and may become a fluid-filled cavity. Coagulative necrosis is the usual pattern after ischaemia in most other solid organs, such as the heart, which is why it is a tempting distractor. Caseous necrosis is typical of tuberculosis. Fat necrosis is seen in acute pancreatitis and breast trauma.

questions.q: State Virchow's triad and apply it to explain why a patient who is immobile after major orthopaedic surgery is at increased risk of deep vein thrombosis.
markScheme: Abnormal blood flow: stasis or turbulence
Vessel wall: endothelial injury
Blood constituents: hypercoagulability
Application: immobility gives venous stasis in the legs; surgery and handling can injure veins
Application: surgery and tissue trauma create a hypercoagulable state; all three components can coexist
questions.modelAnswer: Virchow's triad describes three factors that predispose to thrombosis: abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), injury to the vessel wall (endothelial damage), and changes in the blood that make it more likely to clot (hypercoagulability). After major orthopaedic surgery, such as hip replacement, the patient is immobile, so the calf muscle pump is less active and blood stagnates in the deep leg veins (stasis). Surgery near the veins, positioning and manipulation of the limb can damage the vessel wall. Tissue trauma and the body's response to surgery increase coagulability. With all three components present, the risk of deep vein thrombosis is high, which is why these patients are assessed for venous thromboembolism risk and given preventive measures.

questions.q: A drug with an elimination half-life of 6 hours is started as a regular maintenance regimen with no loading dose. Approximately when will its plasma concentration reach steady state?
options: It cannot reach steady state without a loading dose
questions.why: Steady state is reached after about 4–5 half-lives, here 24–30 hours, regardless of the dose. Six hours is one half-life, when the concentration is only about 50% of its eventual steady-state value. Twelve hours is two half-lives, about 75% of steady state. A loading dose only gets to the target concentration sooner; regular dosing reaches steady state without one.

questions.q: What does a competitive antagonist do to the dose–response curve of an agonist acting on the same receptor?
options: Lowers the maximum response without shifting it
Turns the agonist into a partial agonist
Shifts it to the right with the maximum response unchanged
questions.why: A competitive antagonist competes reversibly for the same binding site, so more agonist is needed for the same effect (a rightward shift), but high agonist concentrations can still reach the full maximum. A leftward shift would mean the agonist had become more potent, the opposite of antagonism. Lowering the maximum is the signature of a non-competitive or irreversible antagonist. Efficacy is a property of the agonist–receptor interaction; an antagonist does not convert the agonist into a partial agonist.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by bioavailability and first-pass metabolism, and why some drugs are given by a route other than oral.
markScheme: Bioavailability: fraction of dose reaching the systemic circulation unchanged (100% IV)
First-pass metabolism: metabolism in the gut wall and liver (via the portal circulation) before the drug reaches the systemic circulation
Extensive first-pass metabolism lowers oral bioavailability
Other routes (e.g. sublingual, intravenous, transdermal) bypass the portal circulation; example such as sublingual glyceryl trinitrate
questions.modelAnswer: Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged; it is 100% by definition for an intravenous dose. A drug swallowed and absorbed from the gut passes through the gut wall and then, via the hepatic portal vein, through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation. Metabolism at these sites is called first-pass metabolism, and when it is extensive it greatly lowers oral bioavailability. Routes that bypass the portal circulation, such as sublingual, intravenous or transdermal administration, avoid this. For example, glyceryl trinitrate is given sublingually so that it is absorbed directly into the systemic circulation, and the intravenous route is used when a rapid, complete and predictable effect is needed.

questions.q:
A randomised controlled trial compares a new treatment with standard care in 4000 adults at risk of heart attack (2000 per group). Over 3 years, 160 patients in the standard care group and 120 in the treatment group have a heart attack.
(a) Calculate the event rate in each group, the relative risk, the relative risk reduction, the absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat. [6]
(b) The 95% confidence interval for the absolute risk reduction is approximately 0.4% to 3.6%. Interpret this, and explain what it implies for statistical significance and for the range of plausible NNTs. [4]
(c) Describe four features of the trial's design and conduct you would check before trusting the result. [6]
(d) A pharmaceutical advertisement says the drug 'cuts heart attacks by 25%'. Explain why this could mislead a patient, and how you would present the benefit instead. [4]
markScheme: (a) RR = 6/8 = 0.75; RRR = 25%; ARR = 2 percentage points; NNT = 1/0.02 = 50 over 3 years
(b) Data compatible with ARR between 0.4% and 3.6%; excludes 0, so significant at the 5% level (p < 0.05)
(b) NNT plausibly from about 28 to about 250: benefit may be modest
(c) Randomisation with concealed allocation; blinding of patients, clinicians and outcome assessors; comparable baseline characteristics
(c) Intention-to-treat analysis and low or balanced loss to follow-up; pre-specified primary outcome; adverse effects; generalisability to the patient
(d) 25% is a relative reduction; the absolute reduction is only 2 percentage points (8% to 6%), NNT 50 over 3 years
(d) Present absolute risks with and without treatment, NNT, harms and costs, in natural frequencies (e.g. 8 vs 6 in 100)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Control event rate = 160/2000 = 0.08 (8%). Experimental event rate = 120/2000 = 0.06 (6%). Relative risk = 0.06/0.08 = 0.75. Relative risk reduction = 1 − 0.75 = 25%. Absolute risk reduction = 0.08 − 0.06 = 0.02 (2 percentage points). Number needed to treat = 1/0.02 = 50: fifty patients must be treated for 3 years to prevent one heart attack.

(b) The confidence interval means the data are compatible with a true absolute reduction anywhere from about 0.4 to 3.6 percentage points. Because the interval excludes zero, the result is statistically significant at the 5% level. Converting the limits, the plausible NNT ranges from about 1/0.036 ≈ 28 to 1/0.004 = 250, so the true benefit might be worthwhile or quite small, and other factors such as side effects and cost become important.

(c) I would check: that allocation was truly random and concealed, so clinicians could not influence who got which treatment; that the groups were similar at baseline; that patients, clinicians and especially outcome assessors were blinded, since diagnosing a heart attack involves judgement; that the analysis was by intention to treat and follow-up was nearly complete in both groups; that the primary outcome was pre-specified rather than chosen after seeing the data; that adverse effects were reported; and that the trial population (age, sex, risk level, setting) resembles my patients, so the result is generalisable.

(d) '25%' is the relative risk reduction. It sounds large, but the absolute benefit is a fall from 8 to 6 heart attacks per 100 people over 3 years, an absolute reduction of 2 percentage points, or one heart attack prevented for every 50 people treated. Relative figures exaggerate the benefit for low-risk patients. I would present natural frequencies (out of 100 people like you, about 8 would have a heart attack without the drug and about 6 with it), alongside the likely side effects, burden and cost, and support the patient to decide in line with their own values, which is the essence of shared, evidence-based decision-making.

questions.q:
A 64-year-old woman is recovering on the ward three days after a hip replacement. She develops a swollen, tender left calf and, the next day, sudden breathlessness and sharp chest pain worse on breathing in.
(a) Using Virchow's triad, explain why she developed a deep vein thrombosis. [5]
(b) Explain how the deep vein thrombosis led to her chest symptoms, and why lung infarction does not occur in every pulmonary embolus. [5]
(c) Outline the imaging investigations commonly used to confirm deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and one radiation-safety consideration. [5]
(d) Describe, in principle, how the risk of venous thromboembolism is reduced in surgical patients. (Doses are not required.) [5]
markScheme: (a) Stasis from immobility and reduced calf muscle pump; endothelial injury from surgery or limb manipulation; hypercoagulability after surgery and tissue trauma
(a) Age and major orthopaedic surgery as additional risk factors; thrombus forms in deep calf veins and can propagate
(b) Thrombus fragments, embolises through the right heart into the pulmonary arteries: pulmonary embolism, causing ventilation–perfusion mismatch and breathlessness

(b) Pleuritic pain suggests pleural irritation from a peripheral infarct; dual supply (pulmonary and bronchial arteries) means many emboli do not cause infarction; infarcts that occur are often haemorrhagic

(c) Compression (duplex) ultrasound of leg veins for DVT; CT pulmonary angiography for PE (ventilation–perfusion scanning an alternative, e.g. if contrast unsuitable); chest X-ray often normal but excludes other causes
(c) Radiation safety: justification under IR(ME)R and checking pregnancy status; ultrasound avoids ionising radiation (contrast allergy and renal function are separate checks before contrast CT)
(d) Risk assessment on admission; early mobilisation and hydration; mechanical prophylaxis (e.g. graduated compression stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression)
(d) Pharmacological prophylaxis with an anticoagulant when indicated after weighing bleeding risk, following guidance (e.g. NICE)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Virchow's triad identifies three contributors to thrombosis, and all are present. Stasis: after hip surgery she is relatively immobile, so the calf muscle pump that normally propels venous blood is inactive and blood pools in the deep veins. Endothelial injury: surgery near the femoral vessels, positioning and manipulation of the leg can damage the vein wall. Hypercoagulability: tissue trauma and the response to surgery increase the tendency of the blood to clot. Her age adds risk. A thrombus forms in the deep veins of the calf, causing swelling and tenderness, and may extend proximally.

(b) Part of the thrombus can break off as an embolus. It travels in the venous return through the right atrium and ventricle into the pulmonary arteries, where it lodges: a pulmonary embolism. Obstructing pulmonary blood flow creates ventilation–perfusion mismatch, lowering oxygenation and causing breathlessness. Sharp pain on inspiration suggests pleural irritation, often from a small peripheral infarct. The lung has a dual blood supply (pulmonary arteries and bronchial arteries), so many emboli do not cause infarction; when infarcts do occur they are typically red (haemorrhagic) because blood continues to enter the damaged tissue.

(c) A deep vein thrombosis is usually confirmed with compression (duplex) ultrasound of the leg veins, which uses no ionising radiation. Pulmonary embolism is commonly confirmed by CT pulmonary angiography; a ventilation–perfusion scan is an alternative, for example when iodinated contrast is unsuitable. A chest radiograph is often normal in PE but helps to exclude other causes such as pneumothorax or pneumonia. Radiation safety: under IR(ME)R the exposure must be justified and pregnancy status checked. Separately, contrast allergy and kidney function should be checked before contrast CT.

(d) Surgical patients should have their risk of venous thromboembolism and of bleeding assessed on admission and reassessed, as NICE guidance recommends. Measures include early mobilisation and adequate hydration; mechanical prophylaxis such as graduated compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression where appropriate; and pharmacological prophylaxis with an anticoagulant when the risk of thrombosis outweighs the risk of bleeding, continued for a period that depends on the type of surgery, according to current guidance and the BNF.
